title: Cassava Dough
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Cassava grated very fine, put in a sack under a stone and left to drain two or three days until it is a dry, tightly pressed clump.
longDesc: This is the prerequisite for akple and the component half of banku, and it is almost nothing but patience. The original directions she worked from are four lines: peel cassava, wash it, grate it very fine, mix water if not too wet, put it in a sack with a stone or a heavy pot on top, and let it drain for two to three days. Her own version uses about two and a half cups of grated cassava and half a cup of water, grated on the fine side of a box grater, swished with water, and drained in a pillowcase under a weighted bowl. The endpoint is a dry, tightly pressed clump.
ingredients: // Yields roughly 2 1/2 cups grated cassava before draining
equipment: A stone or heavy weighted pot or bowl
steps: Peel the cassava and wash it. Ask the shop to cut a tuber across so you can check it is fresh.
Grate it very fine — roll up your sleeves and use some elbow grease.
Mix in water if it is not too wet, and swish it.
Put it in a sack or pillowcase.
Put a stone, a heavy pot or a weighted bowl on top, over a catch pan.
// ENDPOINT: a dry, tightly pressed-together clump of cassava.
Blend with water to a dough or paste when you need it.
chefTips: The endpoint is a dry, tightly pressed clump — that is the only cue given and it is enough. If it is still wet and loose it needs longer under the weight.
Grate on the FINE side. Coarse grating will not press down into a usable dough.
Two to three days under a real weight. A light bowl will not do it.
Ask the shop to cut a tuber across so you can see whether it is fresh. Her own advice, and cassava goes off invisibly from the inside.
This is draining, not fermenting. Neither of the two posts describing it calls it fermentation or gives a sour or smell cue — which matters for akple, where the author says the dough is unfermented.
Catch pan underneath. A surprising volume of starchy liquid comes out.
Blend with about a cup of water when you come to use it — that is the quantity in the akple recipe.
commonMistakes: Too little weight on the sack.
Draining for one day and calling it done.
Treating the drain as a fermentation and waiting for sourness.
Using cassava that has gone off, which is not visible from the outside.
servedWith: Used as a component, not eaten alone
sources: Adapted from 'Recipe #76: Cassava (yucca) dough', betumiblog.blogspot.com, Thursday 7 July 2011. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 1:47 PM'. NO YIELD is printed.

THE ORIGINAL DIRECTIONS she worked from, quoted and TWO-PASS: 'Peel cassava, wash it, grate it very fine, mix water if not too wet, put in a sack and put a stone or heavy pot on it and let drain for 2-3 days.'

HER OWN VERSION, SINGLE-PASS and therefore unverified: about 2½ cups grated cassava and about ½ cup water. She grates on the fine side of a box grater, swishes it with water, puts it in a pillowcase with a weighted bowl on top over a catch pan, and drains 2-3 days. She began with about 1 pound of peeled cassava.

Quoted from a second fetch: 'Roll up your sleeves and use some elbow grease to grate the cassava into a clean bowl.' And: 'On Saturday I'll take it out and see what we have'. Her source is described as 'sketchy directions in my notes', WITH NO NAMED TEACHER.

THE ENDPOINT comes from the follow-up akple post, verbatim: 'After 3 days, you will have a dry, tightly pressed together clump of cassava.' This post says 2-3 days of weighted draining; the akple post says 3. Both are recorded.

NOT A FERMENTATION, and this is the point worth stating: NEITHER POST CALLS THIS FERMENTING, and neither gives a souring, smell or bubble cue. It is a mechanical dewatering. That is consistent with the author's statement at GHA042 that akple is made from unfermented corn dough, and it means this preparation needs no fermentation endpoint.
A FRESHNESS TIP, SINGLE-PASS: she advises asking produce staff to cut tubers so you can check freshness.

FOR CONTRAST, a genuinely fermented cassava preparation with full endpoints is at GHA035 (akyeke), where grated cassava ferments 5-7 days to pH 3.21 with a documented texture change. The difference between that and this two-day drain is the difference between a fermentation and a pressing.
storage: Use within a day or two of draining, or freeze.
reheating: Not applicable — it is a raw component.
healthBenefits: Draining removes a portion of cassava's water-soluble cyanogenic compounds.
culturalNote: Cassava dough under a stone in a sack for three days is the kind of preparation that sits behind half of West African cooking and almost never gets written down, because it is not a recipe so much as a household routine. That this version was reconstructed from sketchy notes, with no teacher named, is itself a small record of how nearly it went undocumented.
